Chapter Two: The First Steps Toward the Sky—Friendship, Failure, and Small Victories.
You know, the journey from curiosity to actually accomplishing something big... it's almost never a straight line. Especially when you don't have much to work with, and the world around you seems like it couldn't care less.
In Coalwood, this small group of friends who dared to dream about building rockets, well, they ran into obstacles at every single turn. Their early attempts? Honestly, they were mostly just trial and error—mostly error, if we're being real. That first rocket they put together from whatever scraps they could find? It fizzled out the moment they lit it. The disappointment hit hard, but it never stuck around for long. There was just something irresistible about the whole process: the planning, the building, and that nervous excitement right before each launch.
With every setback, their friendship grew even stronger. Each of them had their own reason for being part of the project. One loved the challenge, another was hoping to find a way out of life in the mine, and another simply wanted to belong to something bigger than himself.
Together, they became a team—each guy bringing his own skills to the table. Some were better at math, some had a real knack for tinkering, and a few could even talk adults into giving up much-needed supplies.
School turned into a sort of battleground. A lot of teachers brushed off their work as just a silly distraction, but one science teacher saw something different. She quietly encouraged their curiosity, giving advice and even letting them borrow books that opened up whole new worlds. Her support was subtle but steady. Sometimes, all it takes is the right mentor to change everything. The boys started spending hours in the library, digging through diagrams and formulas, trying to wrap their heads around the science of propulsion and flight.
Back at home, things got tense between the boy and his dad. His father, practical and proud, just couldn't understand why his son would risk so much for a dream that, to him, seemed impossible. His mom, though, became an ally—helping in quiet ways, smoothing over arguments or just giving her son a safe place to talk things out.
The reaction around town was all over the place. Some neighbors watched the boys’ rocket launches and just laughed, while others looked on with suspicion. A few even warned them to stop before someone got hurt. But as the rockets started flying higher and farther, people’s curiosity began to turn into admiration. Those launches became little events in their own right—crowds would gather, cheering when things went well and groaning when they didn’t.
Then came the afternoon when a launch went so wrong it left a crater smack in the middle of a neighbor’s yard. That was their first real crisis. The threat of serious punishment hung over them, and for a split second, it seemed like their dream might just be over. But instead of walking away, they regrouped. They learned the importance of asking for permission, planning more carefully, and owning up to their mistakes. It became clear—failure wasn’t the end. It was just part of the journey.
As months went by, folks started calling them the “rocket boys.” That little nickname carried both a sense of pride and a whole lot of pressure. The stakes felt higher, but so did the rewards. Every single successful launch was proof that with enough determination, even the wildest dreams could really take flight.
